title: The real cost of scams isn't just money, it's trust
summary: Written by Shamina Singh, founder and president of the Mastercard Center for Inclusive Growth and the EVP for Sustainability at Mastercard and Ilaria Chan, founding Chairwoman of Tech For Good…

blocks.text: Written by Shamina Singh, founder and president of the Mastercard Center for Inclusive Growth and the EVP for Sustainability at Mastercard and Ilaria Chan, founding Chairwoman of Tech For Good Institute
Filipinos are among Southeast Asia’s savviest scam spotters. But recognizing a scam and being resilient to one are two different things.

As more technologies, like AI, are coming online, bad actors can now write convincing messages, clone voices, and run scams at industrial scale. Many may think scams are just a security problem, but it’s much more. When people are victims of scams, trust in the digital system weakens, leading to lower participation in the digital economy. And for someone new to digital finance, one scam can wipe out their savings and their willingness to go digital again.

Across Southeast Asia, that trust is increasingly at risk. According to a new report from the Tech for Good Institute, Filipinos correctly identified 80% of scam scenarios, compared with 71% across Southeast Asia. But the broader findings reveal a more complicated challenge: recognizing a scam does not necessarily mean knowing where to turn when something goes wrong. And worse, many do not have a path towards redress when they become victims of a scam.

The report, supported by the Mastercard Center for Inclusive Growth, analyzes survey data from 6,000 people in Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. The survey shows that scams are now built into everyday digital life in the region, but consumers and small business owners are ill-equipped to protect themselves against it. Six in ten people surveyed encountered a scam in the past year. More than half of those affected lost money, personal information or access to an account. Meanwhile, nearly two in three people say scams are getting harder to spot.

The financial toll is also serious. TFGI’s earlier regional research cites data from the Global Anti Scams Alliance estimating that Southeast Asians lost US$23.6 billion to scams in 2024 alone, money taken from households, small businesses and the region’s growing digital economy.
The findings point to a challenge larger than fraud prevention: if people no longer feel safe participating online, the region’s digital growth cannot be fully inclusive.
Recognition is not resilience

The people most at risk aren’t necessarily who we think. Adults aged 18–34 are more than twice as likely as those over 50 to have lost something to a scam (46% vs. 21%), suggesting exposure is tied more closely to digital activity and participation, rather than conventional assumptions of vulnerability, such as age or inexperience.

Vulnerability also takes different forms: nearly three in ten respondents are what TFGI calls the “Overconfident Vulnerable,” whose confidence runs ahead of their ability to recognize scams. When contacted by a fake government or police official, this group spots the scam only 37% of the time.

Across the region, only 42% of people feel confident spotting a scam and just 53% know where to report one. That gap has consequences: nearly one in five respondents say scam concerns have caused them to cut back on online banking or e-wallets, rising to nearly one in four among scam victims. In the Philippines, nearly three in ten now use cash more often than digital payments. And with 43% across Southeast Asia feeling left to manage scam risks on their own, awareness alone isn’t enough.

The Philippines shows the confidence-skills gap clearly. Despite leading the region in spotting scams, only 39% say they feel confident in doing so. And when faced with a fake government or police message, only 29% chose the safest response, such as verifying through an official website or hotline. Recognizing scams is not the same as being equipped to respond to them. People need trusted ways to report scams, seek help and recover when something goes wrong.

This challenge will be part of the conversation when leaders from government, business, philanthropy and civil society gather in Manila on November 11 for the second annual ASEAN Inclusive Growth Summit. The setting matters because scam resilience cannot be built by one institution or sector alone. It requires the same kind of cross-sector cooperation needed to ensure the region’s digital transformation remains inclusive.
Building scam resilience together
Two priorities can help Southeast Asia build a more resilient response.

Firstly, scams are a network issue, so our response needs to extend across the network, too. A single scam can move from a text message to a messaging app to an e-wallet transfer in minutes, with no one institution seeing the whole picture. Banks, telecoms, digital platforms, regulators and law enforcement need to be able to share intelligence and coordinate their response.

We already have models to build on. To streamline scam reporting and response efforts, the Philippines recently took a first step with the launch of a new anti-scam hotline. Singapore’s ScamShield gives people a centralized place to report scams and seek help, while Malaysia’s National Scam Response Centre brings police, the central bank and regulators together in a coordinated response. The next step is to strengthen that cooperation across institutions and borders.

Secondly, once a scam occurs, people need to know where to turn. Alongside, the institutions protecting them need to learn and adapt as quickly as scammers do. That means clear reporting channels, coordinated responses when accounts are compromised and practical guidance that reflects how scams happen. It also means measuring success by more than losses prevented. If fear of scams causes people to retreat from digital banking and e-wallets, for example, we have protected an account but lost something equally important: trust.

Ultimately, resilience isn’t measured only by whether a scam is stopped. It’s also measured by whether people still trust the system after something goes wrong. A truly resilient system helps people report and recover without blame, learns from their experiences and gives them the confidence to keep participating in the digital economy.

When leaders gather in Manila for the ASEAN Inclusive Growth Summit, scam resilience should be treated as essential to the region’s inclusive-growth agenda and dialogue. Southeast Asia has spent years bringing more people into the digital economy. Now we need to make sure they have every reason to stay. Protecting people’s confidence, as well as their money, is how we ensure the region’s digital transformation remains safe, resilient and open to everyone.
